passage_text:
Researchers at the University of Greenfield investigated the effect of a novel dietary supplement, NutriBoost, on the metabolic rate of adult mice. The study enrolled 60 mice, randomly assigned to three groups: a control group receiving standard chow (n=20), a low-dose group receiving 5 mg/kg of NutriBoost (n=20), and a high-dose group receiving 15 mg/kg of NutriBoost (n=20). Over a 12-week period, researchers measured the resting metabolic rate (RMR) of each mouse weekly using indirect calorimetry. The table below summarizes the mean RMR (in kilocalories per day) and standard deviation (SD) for each group at the end of the study.

Table 3-4
| Group          | Mean RMR (kcal/day) | SD (kcal/day) |
|----------------|---------------------|----------------|
| Control        | 12.4                | 1.2            |
| Low-dose       | 13.1                | 1.4            |
| High-dose      | 14.5                | 1.6            |
stem: Based on the data presented, which statement best describes the effect of NutriBoost on the mice’s resting metabolic rate?

options.A: NutriBoost had no significant effect on RMR compared to the control group.
options.B: The low-dose group had a higher RMR than the control group, but the high-dose group did not.
options.C: Both low- and high-dose groups had higher RMRs than the control group, with the high-dose group showing the greatest increase.
options.D: Only the high-dose group had a statistically significant increase in RMR compared to the control group.

explanation: The mean RMR values show a clear dose-dependent increase: 12.4 (control) < 13.1 (low-dose) < 14.5 (high-dose). Both experimental groups exceed the control, and the high-dose group has the largest mean difference, indicating a dose-dependent effect.
trap: Assuming the larger high-dose difference is statistically significant, although the table gives only means and SDs and no test or p-value.

| Control        | 12.4                | 1.2            |
| Low-dose       | 13.1                | 1.4            |
| High-dose      | 14.5                | 1.6            |
stem: Which of the following best describes an appropriate control for this experiment?

options.A: A group of mice receiving a placebo supplement identical in appearance to NutriBoost.
options.B: A group of mice receiving a higher dose of NutriBoost than the high-dose group.
options.C: A group of mice receiving a different dietary supplement known to increase RMR.
options.D: A group of mice that are not monitored for RMR during the study period.

explanation: Correct: A placebo group handled and dosed identically isolates the effect of NutriBoost itself. Why the others are wrong: B) a higher dose is another treatment level, not a control. C) a different RMR-raising supplement adds a new variable. D) not measuring RMR removes the outcome data.
trap: Choosing a higher dose as the control, which confounds dose with control.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: The high-dose increase in RMR is statistically significant (p < 0.05).
options.B: The high-dose group shows the largest mean RMR.
options.C: The standard deviation of RMR is larger in the high-dose group than in the control group.
options.D: The low-dose group’s RMR is lower than the high-dose group’s RMR.

explanation: The table gives only means and SDs, with no p-values or tests, so statistical significance cannot be concluded. The ordering of means, the high-dose maximum, and the larger high-dose SD (1.6 vs 1.2) are all directly shown.
trap: Treating a larger mean difference as proof of statistical significance.

| Control        | 12.4                | 1.2            |
| Low-dose       | 13.1                | 1.4            |
| High-dose      | 14.5                | 1.6            |
stem: Using the pooled SD (equal group sizes), what is Cohen's d for the difference in mean RMR between the high-dose and control groups?
explanation: Correct: C) Pooled SD = √((1.2² + 1.6²)/2) = √2.0 = 1.41; d = (14.5 − 12.4)/1.41 = 1.49. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.49 divides the low-dose difference (0.7) by this pooled SD, so it is not the high-dose comparison. B) 1.31 divides by the high-dose SD only (2.1/1.6). D) 1.75 divides by the control SD only (2.1/1.2).
trap: Dividing the mean difference by one group's SD instead of the pooled SD.
